clinicalPearls: A variant of fibroadenoma occurring predominantly in adolescents and young women, characterised by increased stromal cellularity and epithelial hyperplasia.
Tends to grow more rapidly and reach a larger size than the common adult fibroadenoma; large lesions are termed giant juvenile fibroadenoma.
Presents as a firm, mobile, painless mass that may cause obvious breast asymmetry, skin stretching and dilated overlying veins.
Rapid growth can compress and displace surrounding normal breast tissue rather than invading it.
Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice in this young age group, showing a well-defined solid mass.
The principal differential on core biopsy is a benign phyllodes tumour, which juvenile fibroadenoma can closely resemble.
Treatment is enucleation or excision, preserving the developing breast and nipple where possible; the outlook is excellent.
Despite alarming size and rapid growth, it is entirely benign with negligible malignant potential.
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile fibroadenoma is a benign biphasic fibroepithelial tumour arising from the hormone-responsive stroma of the terminal duct lobular unit, most likely reflecting an exaggerated proliferative response to the hormonal milieu of adolescence. It differs from the ordinary adult fibroadenoma in its greater stromal cellularity and its pericanalicular growth pattern with florid, sometimes gynaecomastoid, epithelial hyperplasia. This heightened cellular activity drives the characteristic rapid enlargement and large size, yet the stroma lacks the atypia, mitotic activity, leaf-like architecture and overgrowth that define a phyllodes tumour, so the lesion remains benign.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia forming a mass
additionalInvestigations: Clinical breast examination with documentation of size and asymmetry
Breast ultrasound as first-line imaging in adolescents
Core needle biopsy to characterise the fibroepithelial lesion
Histology assessing stromal cellularity, atypia and architecture
MRI in very large lesions to plan excision
Follow-up imaging to confirm stability or excision completeness
Multidisciplinary review if phyllodes tumour cannot be excluded
redFlags: Very rapid enlargement with skin compromise or ulceration
Histological features raising the possibility of a phyllodes tumour
Stromal overgrowth or mitotic activity on biopsy
Skin changes or fixity atypical for a benign lesion
reference.prognosis: Juvenile fibroadenoma is benign with an excellent prognosis after complete excision, and malignant transformation is not a feature. Recurrence is uncommon, though further fibroadenomas may develop elsewhere in the breast over time.
pitfalls: Misclassifying a benign phyllodes tumour as juvenile fibroadenoma on limited biopsy
Delaying excision of a large lesion and allowing further distortion of the developing breast
Performing overly aggressive surgery that damages the breast bud or nipple in an adolescent
Confusing the lesion with virginal breast hypertrophy
Assuming rapid growth implies malignancy and causing unnecessary alarm

management: Confirm the benign fibroepithelial nature with ultrasound-guided core biopsy to distinguish it from a phyllodes tumour before deciding treatment
Excise (enucleate) large or giant lesions and those causing asymmetry or overlying skin compromise
Preserve the developing breast bud and normal breast tissue during surgery in adolescents and use oncoplastic techniques for large defects
Observe small, asymptomatic, radiologically typical lesions with interval ultrasound follow-up
Provide reassurance about the benign course and negligible malignant potential
Arrange follow-up imaging to confirm stability or completeness of excision and to detect further fibroadenomas
